title: Why Quick Compensation Hasn't Replaced Eaton Fire Lawsuits—So Far
gist: RAND researchers find Southern California Edison's direct-payment Wildfire Recovery Compensation Program pays Eaton fire survivors far faster (offers in 36 days on average) and often without lawyers, but covers only about 25% of destroyed properties and has not displaced litigation. They propose design fixes for future programs.

insights.claim: As of Oct. 1, 2026, Edison's Eaton fire compensation program had received 5,000 claims, made 2,900 offers, and about 80% of offers were accepted.
insights.speaker: Lloyd Dixon
insights.so_what: Gauges uptake and acceptance; high acceptance suggests offers are broadly acceptable to those who engage.
insights.locator: As of Oct. 1, the Edison program received 5,000 claims

insights.claim: The average calculated compensation per destroyed-home claim through September was $1.95 million, with just over $850,000 paid by Edison after insurance was deducted.
insights.speaker: Lloyd Dixon
insights.so_what: Sizes Edison's per-home cash outlay after insurance offsets, a key input for utility liability and ratepayer exposure.
insights.locator: The average calculated compensation due per claim

insights.claim: Edison made offers in 36 days on average once claims were substantially complete, versus years of litigation after the Thomas and Woolsey fires.
insights.speaker: Lloyd Dixon
insights.so_what: Speed is the program's clearest advantage over tort litigation and reduces claimant and court strain.

insights.claim: About 60% of program claims involve no attorney, indicating direct-payment programs can cut legal costs for claimants.
insights.speaker: Lloyd Dixon
insights.so_what: Lower legal costs shrink total transaction costs that ultimately partly fall on ratepayers.
insights.locator: About 60% of claims submitted do not involve an attorney

insights.claim: With two months left, program claims cover only about 25% of the nearly 6,000 properties with destroyed structures, while tens of thousands of parties pursue claims in court, so the program is not a broad substitute for lawsuits.
insights.speaker: Lloyd Dixon
insights.so_what: Edison's litigation liability remains large and slow-resolving; the first Eaton trial is scheduled for January 2027, a catalyst to watch.
insights.locator: We estimate that with only two months left

insights.claim: Eaton fire litigation is on a timetable similar to Thomas and Woolsey: more than two years to set mediation protocols plus additional years to work through claims, with the first trial set for January 2027.
insights.speaker: Lloyd Dixon
insights.so_what: Long litigation tails imply prolonged uncertainty for Edison's liabilities and ratepayer burden.
insights.locator: Eaton fire cases are on a similar timetable

insights.claim: Some claimants see the fast-pay offers as falling short on rebuilding costs, loss-of-use payments or noneconomic losses compared with potential litigation outcomes.
insights.speaker: Lloyd Dixon
insights.so_what: Perceived undervaluation of noneconomic damages is a key brake on opt-in; settlement values may rise via detailed review.
insights.locator: Some found them reasonable; others perceived shortfalls

insights.claim: The program pays only the gap between available insurance and calculated loss, whereas litigation payments reflect actual insurance recoveries, which can leave claimants in insurance disputes worse off.
insights.speaker: Lloyd Dixon
insights.so_what: Insurance-offset design affects both claimant uptake and what utilities ultimately pay.
insights.locator: Another obstacle is that the program only pays

insights.claim: Trust and timing limit uptake: Edison designs and administers the program, raising objectivity concerns, and it opened nearly 10 months after the fire, by which time many had retained counsel.
insights.speaker: Lloyd Dixon
insights.so_what: Utility-run compensation faces structural credibility and timing handicaps.

insights.claim: RAND recommends future fire compensation programs launch quickly, use a neutral administrator, base insurance offsets on actual payouts rather than available coverage, and offer advances on expected settlements.
insights.speaker: Lloyd Dixon
insights.so_what: Template for utility wildfire compensation legislation and programs.
insights.quote: Launch quickly. Have a neutral program administrator. Base insurance offsets on actual payouts.

insights.claim: Streamlining court approval of settlements involving minors, such as one judge per family, and encouraging survivors to pursue program offers during litigation could speed payments.
insights.speaker: Lloyd Dixon
insights.so_what: Court-process fixes are a lever to accelerate payouts without new legislation.
insights.locator: Settlements involving children require court approval

insights.claim: Capping noneconomic damages in wildfire property claims could temper open-ended judgment expectations but would also shrink some survivors' compensation and affect community recovery speed.
insights.speaker: Lloyd Dixon
insights.so_what: A cap would reduce utility tail liability; watch legislative proposals.
insights.locator: it is worth weighing whether it makes sense to cap noneconomic damages

insights.claim: California's Senate Bill 492, a package of utility liability and survivor compensation reforms including a fast-pay process, did not pass in the latest session, but lessons from Edison's program should inform future legislation.
insights.speaker: Lloyd Dixon
insights.so_what: Utility liability reform remains unresolved in California; expect renewed bills.
